newsitem.title: UK: European markets hungry for deal on tight EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: European markets hungry for deal on tight EMU pact.

text.p: Europe's financial markets were watching for signs that an agreement on tough budgetary discipline would emerge from a meeting of European Union finance ministers in Brussels on Monday, economists said.

If such signals materialised, bond markets in particular would be cheered, viewing a fiscally tight budgetary pact after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) as something to balance out the "creative accounting" being allowed for countries to meet the single currency criteria.
But if noises from Brussels suggested a soft disciplinary approach to the so-called stability pact, worries would grow.

"The key issue is whether the Germans win their demand for a very strict, mechanical fining structure or whether we move towards the more liberal approach favoured by many of the other members," said Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International in London.
Financial markets needed some reassurance, analysts said, that laxity and sloppy interpretation of the rules would not infect the process towards EMU.

"The markets will want something pretty tight for the simple reason that the EU Commission effectively legalised the fiscal "window dressing' we saw from the likes of France and Italy," said Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets in London.

Italy and France were seen by markets as using "creative accounting" in their 1997 budget proposals in an effort to meet critical deficit targets laid down in the Maastricht Treaty. The treaty calls for budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.

France factored a one-off payment from France Telecom into its budget deficit reduction. Italy plans to introduce a one-off 12.5 trillion lire ($8.3 billion) "Euro-tax" to help it on its way to the first round of EMU, slated for January 1999.
"We need some kind of compensation effect, and that would be a very rigourous fiscal stability pact," said Roberts.

But efforts to finalise plans for a stability pact have proved one of the most tricky corners to negotiate on the path to EMU, with Germany and the Netherlands facing opposition from most other EU members on calls for a strict fining system if deficit and other limits are violated.
Analysts said it was unlikely any concrete decision would be taken at Monday's finance ministers' meeting and the Dublin EU summit on December 13-14 was more likely to mark the date for an agreement.

Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London, said the main issue for peripheral European bond markets, the biggest beneficiaries so far from recent EMU optimism, was that at least some positive noises emerged on an agreement.
"The real risk for the markets is that they don't come to any agreement," she said. "That could prompt some profit-taking eventually."
If Germany and the Netherlands win through, European bond markets across the board would have something to cheer about, analysts said.
"A tight agreement would put to rest fears that the whole EMU process is going to involve watering down," said IBJ's Hannah.
And he said further speculative fuel would be added to the fire if such an agreement were reached.

"If Germany gets its way on a tough stability pact, there will be a lot of speculation that some kind of deal has been done between Germany and France -- that if France supports the tough line, Germany will scratch their back later on," he said.

Recent debate in France about the franc's strength against the dollar, which is hampering economic recovery, has sparked market talk that German interest rates may have to be lowered to allow the Bank of France to follow suit.
Agreement on a tight post-EMU fining structure would inspire even more speculation, analysts said.

"A tough approach on the stability pact is essentially a tightening of future fiscal policy," Hannah said. "That would mean lower real interest rates which is necessarily euro negative and dollar positive."
If, in addition, a Franco-German deal led to a loosening of monetary policy in the run-up to EMU, the case for lower real yields would be reinforced, Hannah said.
